questions.prompt: What actually causes the Moon to go through phases?
options: The Moon's own light output changing
Earth's shadow falling on the Moon
How much of the Moon's always-sunlit half happens to face Earth
Clouds on Earth blocking part of the view
questions.explanation: The Moon reflects sunlight and always has one lit half. As it orbits Earth, the angle between Sun, Moon, and Earth changes — so the amount of that lit half we can actually see from Earth changes too. That's a phase.
questions.misconception: "Earth's shadow" describes a lunar eclipse, a rare, brief event — not the routine month-long phase cycle, which is caused by simple geometry, not any shadow at all.

questions.prompt: At New Moon, why can we barely see the Moon at all?
options: The Moon has moved too far away
The Moon's lit half is facing almost entirely away from Earth
Earth is blocking all sunlight from reaching the Moon
The Moon is not actually in the sky at that time
questions.explanation: At New Moon, the Moon sits roughly between Earth and the Sun, so the side facing us is the Moon's unlit (night) side — it's still there, just not visibly lit from our angle.
questions.misconception: It's tempting to think the Moon disappears or moves away, but it's in the sky the whole time — we just can't see its dark side.

questions.prompt: How long does a full cycle of moon phases (new to new) take?
options: About 1 day
About 7 days
About 29.5 days
About 1 year
questions.explanation: A full phase cycle, called a synodic month, takes about 29.5 days — slightly longer than the Moon's 27.3-day orbit because Earth also moves around the Sun during that time.
questions.misconception: The Moon's 27.3-day orbital period is often quoted as "the phase cycle," but the actual phase cycle is a bit longer because Earth keeps moving too.

questions.prompt: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon, no matter the phase?
options: The Moon does not rotate at all
The Moon is tidally locked — its rotation exactly matches its orbit around Earth
Earth's gravity keeps the same side lit
We don't — the far side is visible during a Full Moon
questions.explanation: The Moon rotates once on its axis in exactly the same time it takes to orbit Earth once, so the same face always points toward us — tidal locking, the same mechanism covered on the Moons branch.
questions.misconception: "Same face always visible" gets misread as "doesn't rotate," but it rotates at exactly the right rate to keep facing us — not zero rotation.

questions.prompt: Which phase comes directly after First Quarter as the Moon continues orbiting toward Full?
options: Waxing Gibbous
New Moon
Waning Gibbous
Last Quarter
questions.explanation: After First Quarter, more and more of the lit half faces Earth on the way to Full Moon — that growing phase is called Waxing Gibbous.
questions.misconception: "Waxing" (growing) and "waning" (shrinking) are easy to mix up — waxing phases lead up to Full Moon, waning phases lead away from it back toward New Moon.
